title: Building The New Equilibrium Economy | NOEMA
gist: Humm argues that AI and robotics may make labor non-scarce for the first time since the Industrial Revolution, and proposes a '30/30 equilibrium' in which ~30% population decline offsets ~30% lower labor demand, with capital deepening (~45% higher capital productivity) lifting GDP per capita 40%+ — a 'shrinking rich' economy whose gains should be shared via public equity stakes in AI infrastructure (a universal capital dividend) rather than inflationary UBI.

insights.claim: Advanced societies are simultaneously spending heavily to compensate for labor shortages (family subsidies, immigration) while investing in technologies designed to eliminate labor altogether.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Policy incoherence: pronatalist/immigration spend may be stranded as AI displaces labor.
insights.quote: Never before has a society simultaneously spent so much money attempting to compensate for labor shortages while investing so much in technologies designed to eliminate labor altogether.

insights.claim: UN projections suggest many Western populations will shrink about 30% by 2100 if current fertility persists and net migration is zero, with Italy approaching a 40%-50% decline.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Long-run demand and fiscal-base shrinkage in Europe; Italy most exposed.

insights.claim: Research cited by Humm finds highly skilled migrants (the minority) generate net economic gains while low-skilled immigration (the majority) can impose a net fiscal drag on advanced welfare states.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Immigration is a weak fix for welfare-state fiscal gaps.

insights.claim: A Silicon Valley pronatalism has emerged — Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and others warn collapsing birth rates threaten civilization — even as their companies build systems to reduce dependence on human labor.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Tech leaders' narratives are internally inconsistent; watch which side policy follows.

insights.claim: South Korea, with fertility around 0.75 and tens of billions spent yearly on birth incentives with little success, is the world's most robot-intensive economy at over 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Korea is the leading indicator for automation substituting a shrinking workforce.
insights.quote: South Korea has become the most robot-intensive economy in the world with over 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers
insights.locator: South Korea, with a fertility rate

insights.claim: Japan, whose working-age population has declined for more than two decades, has over 400 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers versus a world average of about 120-150.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Robotics demand is structurally tied to demographic decline in East Asia.

insights.claim: Humm argues South Korea and Japan offer a preview of the intelligence economy, raising the question of whether demographic decline and automation could become complementary rather than opposing forces.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: East Asia as the testbed for the demographics-automation thesis.
insights.locator: South Korea and Japan offer a preview

themes.theme: The wage-based social contract under strain

insights.claim: Labor accounts for up to 60% of GDP and private consumption for nearly 70% in OECD nations, and wages finance taxation, welfare and pensions.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Fiscal systems are levered to wages; AI displacement directly threatens tax bases.
insights.quote: labor accounts for up to 60% of GDP and private consumption for nearly 70% for OECD nations
insights.locator: This model was at the core

insights.claim: Every productive hour of work finances about nine hours of non-working life across society, a ratio that has risen with shorter working hours and longer life expectancy.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Dependency ratio pressure is already extreme before AI shocks.
insights.quote: Every productive hour finances about nine hours of non-working life

insights.claim: Advanced economies have answered how to finance ever more years of life with ever fewer years of work through a fragile mix of growth and rising public debt — an answer AI may undermine by eroding the labor market.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Sovereign debt sustainability is exposed to AI-driven wage erosion.

insights.claim: Around 1800 roughly 75% of Americans worked in agriculture versus under 2% today; Henry Ford's 1914 wage increase symbolized industrial capitalism binding production, wages and demand.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Historical precedent: wage-demand loop is what AI threatens to break.

themes.theme: AI as abundant intelligence and labor substitution

insights.claim: Every major technological revolution made a scarce factor abundant — fossil fuels for mechanical energy, globalization for physical labor — and AI may now do the same for intelligence.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Cognition becoming cheap reprices knowledge-work-heavy sectors.

insights.claim: Erik Brynjolfsson's 'Turing Trap' and Daron Acemoglu's analysis suggest AI may break the historical pattern of technology creating more jobs than it destroys, since it performs the cognitive work that let workers move up the value chain and firms may choose replacement over augmentation.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Schumpeterian job-creation comfort may not hold; labor-market downside tail risk.

insights.claim: Many of today's most valuable AI companies generate extraordinary market value with remarkably small workforces.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Value-per-employee at AI firms signals capital capture of AI gains.
insights.quote: Many of today’s most valuable AI companies generate extraordinary market value with remarkably small workforces.

insights.claim: Agentic AI accelerates displacement because agents perform entire workflows — analyzing information, correcting errors, adapting strategies and coordinating processes — with minimal human intervention.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Agentic workflow automation is the key driver for white-collar substitution.

insights.claim: In the first, white-collar wave, junior analysts, lawyers, consultants and software engineers in London or New York cost employers 80-100 per hour while language models can do many of their tasks for a fraction of a cent, and software improvements propagate instantly at scale.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Professional services and junior-staff-heavy business models face margin/headcount disruption.

insights.claim: In the second, blue-collar wave, humanoid robot makers such as Tesla and China's Unitree hope to cut operating costs below $2 per hour, versus 30-50 per hour for an average American worker.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Humanoid robotics cost curves are the variable to watch for physical-labor substitution.
insights.quote: Their manufacturers hope eventually to reduce operating costs to below $2 per hour.
insights.locator: The second wave is now reaching

insights.claim: IMF research suggests nearly 60% of jobs in advanced economies will be affected by AI, with almost half facing substantial disruption or substitution; Humm judges a roughly 30% fall in total employment over coming decades no longer implausible.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Plan for large-scale employment contraction scenarios.
insights.quote: Against that background, a reduction of roughly 30% in total employment over the coming decades no longer appears implausible.
insights.locator: Research by the International Monetary Fund

insights.claim: Humm's '30/30 equilibrium' posits that a ~30% population decline over decades could broadly offset a similar AI/robotics-driven fall in labor demand, keeping the labor-to-population ratio stable without extra fiscal burden.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Reframes demographic decline from bearish to potentially stabilizing for aging, automating economies.

insights.claim: Per the Solow-Swan model, offsetting a 30% labor-force decline requires roughly a 45% rise in capital productivity, which would stabilize GDP and raise GDP per capita by more than 40%; Humm argues learning curves in semiconductors, compute, AI and robotics make this unambitious.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Capital deepening (semis, compute, robotics) is the investable engine of per-capita growth.
insights.quote: A 30% decline in the labor force would have to be offset by roughly a 45% increase in capital productivity. This would raise GDP per capita by more than 40%.
insights.locator: If we want an economy’s GDP

insights.claim: Citing the Jevons paradox, Humm predicts we will consume far more AI as it gets cheaper, and that AI 'abundance' carries heavy costs in electricity, compute infrastructure, rare materials and hardware.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Supports sustained demand for power, data centers and critical materials.
insights.quote: As AI becomes cheaper, we will almost certainly consume far more of it.

insights.claim: A 'shrinking-rich economy' may require a monetary and financial system that derives stability from capital productivity rather than ever-expanding debt, since current debt and asset valuations depend on continual expansion.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Long-run challenge to growth-dependent debt dynamics and asset valuations.

insights.claim: The intelligence economy undermines 'big is beautiful' geopolitics because AI makes intelligence abundant and autonomous drones erode traditional military advantages of scale.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Smaller, high-tech states may gain relative power; defense spending shifts to autonomy.

insights.claim: Using Eugene Odum's pioneer vs. climax ecosystems, Humm frames the fossil-fuel economy as humanity's pioneer phase and argues AI plus demographic decline could enable a 'climax society', pointing to robotic recycling, AI-managed precision fermentation and closed material loops.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Circular-economy tech (precision fermentation, robotic recycling) aligned with this thesis.

themes.theme: Who owns the surplus: UBI vs universal capital dividend

insights.claim: If AI and robotics replace labor, income will shift from wages to owners of machines, models, data centers, energy systems and platforms — which also threatens demand, since even the most productive AI economy needs customers who can afford its output.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: AI-driven demand deficiency is a macro risk even for capital owners.

insights.claim: Humm argues universal basic income is a 'pharmakon': debt-financed UBI adds purchasing power without new productive assets and is inflationary, while production-tax-financed UBI gets passed into prices, dissipating the AI productivity dividend either way.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: UBI-heavy policy responses carry inflation risk; watch financing design.

insights.claim: England's 1795 Speenhamland wage-supplement system ended up subsidizing low-paying employers and entrenching the poor's dependence on local authorities, a warning for income-support approaches to a post-labor economy.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Historical precedent against transfer-based settlements.

insights.claim: Humm proposes a universal capital dividend: governments take equity, public or sovereign wealth stakes in AI infrastructure that relies on public resources, data and markets, distributing proceeds directly to citizens — which he claims is non-inflationary.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Watch for state equity stakes in AI infrastructure — dilution/governance risk for AI asset owners.
insights.quote: Society’s claim to a universal capital dividend, instead of a UBI, could take the form of ownership

insights.claim: Because AI models are trained on humanity's accumulated knowledge and depend on publicly funded research and infrastructure, Humm invokes Marx's 'general intellect' to argue society has a claim on AI's productive infrastructure.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Justification narrative for public claims on AI returns is gaining intellectual traction.
insights.quote: The intelligence economy is built by both private firms and a civilizational commons.

themes.theme: Meaning and the atrophy of judgment

insights.claim: Drawing on Hannah Arendt's 'worldlessness' and David Graeber's 'bullshit jobs', Humm argues the deeper post-labor crisis may be meaninglessness rather than unemployment.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Social stability in a post-labor world depends on non-work sources of meaning.

insights.claim: Delegation to AI moves from assisting to recommending to deciding, and human judgment atrophies through disuse — which Humm calls possibly the deepest alignment problem, risking 'Homo algorithmus'.
insights.speaker: PHILIPP HUMM
insights.so_what: Dependency on AI decision systems creates lock-in for platforms and governance risk.
insights.quote: Their purpose is optimization. Ours is judgment. Confusing the two may ultimately prove to be the deepest alignment problem of all.
